entries.436530f6db16056b8b2f5646d9cc6b3439b16d93: <div sID="gen20542" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Nah.2" sID="Nah.2"/> <div eID="gen20542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20543" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20544" type="x-p"/> We now come closer to Nineveh, that great city; she took, not warning by the destruction of her armies and the fall of her king, and therefore may expect, since she persists in her enmity to God, that he will proceed in his controversy with her. Here is foretold, I. The approach of the enemy that should destroy Nineveh, and the terror of his military preparations, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1-Nah.2.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The taking of the city, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">ver. 6</reference>. III. The captivity of the queen, the flight of the inhabitants, the seizing of all its wealth, and the great consternation it should be in, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.7-Nah.2.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. IV. All this is traced up to its true causes—their sinning against God and God's appearing against them, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11-Nah.2.13">ver. 11-13</reference>. All this was fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar, in the first year of his reign, in conjunction with Cyaxares, or Ahasuerus, king of the Medes, conquered Nineveh, and made himself master of the Assyrian monarchy.
entries.d50c5b6f3786f166a73503700a7c0a844b7bab84: <div eID="gen20544" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20543" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Nineveh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make <hi type="italic">thy</hi> loins strong, fortify <hi type="italic">thy</hi> power mightily. <hi type="super">2</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches. <hi type="super">3</hi> The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men <hi type="italic">are</hi> in scarlet: the chariots <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. <hi type="super">4</hi> The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings. <hi type="super">5</hi> He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared. <hi type="super">6</hi> The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead <hi type="italic">her</hi> as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. <hi type="super">8</hi> But Nineveh <hi type="italic">is</hi> of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away. Stand, stand, <hi type="italic">shall they cry;</hi> but none shall look back. <hi type="super">9</hi> Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none end of the store <hi type="italic">and</hi> glory out of all the pleasant furniture. <hi type="super">10</hi> She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain <hi type="italic">is</hi> in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness. <div eID="gen20545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20546" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An alarm of war sent to Nineveh, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">v. 1</reference>. The prophet speaks of it as just at hand, for it is neither doubtful nor far distant: "Look about thee, and see, <hi type="italic">he that dashes in pieces has come up before thy face.</hi> Nebuchadnezzar, who is noted, and will be yet more so, for dashing nations in pieces, begins with thee, and will dissipate and disperse thee;" so some render the word. Babylon is called the <hi type="italic">hammer of the whole earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jer. l. 23</reference>. The attempt of Nebuchadnezzar upon Nineveh is public, bold, and daring: "He <hi type="italic">has come up before thy face,</hi> avowing his design to ruin thee; and therefore stand to thy arms, <hi type="italic">O Nineveh! keep the munition;</hi> secure thy towers and magazines: <hi type="italic">watch the way;</hi> set guards upon all the avenues to the city; <hi type="italic">make thy loins strong;</hi> encourage thy soldiers; animate thyself and them; <hi type="italic">fortify thy power mightily,</hi> as cities do when an enemy is advancing against them" (this is spoken ironically); "do the utmost thou canst, yet thou shalt not be able to put by the stroke of this judgment, for <hi type="italic">there is no counsel or strength against the Lord.</hi>" <div eID="gen20546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20547" type="x-p"/> II. A manifesto published, showing the causes of the war (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel,</hi> that is, 1. The Assyrians have been abusive to Jacob, the two tribes (have humbled and mortified them), as well as to Israel, the ten tribes, <hi type="italic">have emptied them, and marred their vine-branches.</hi> For this God will reckon with them; though done long since, it shall come into the account now against that kingdom, and Nineveh the head-city of it. God's quarrel with them is <hi type="italic">for the violence done to Jacob.</hi> Or, (2.) God is now by Nebuchadnezzar about <hi type="italic">to turn away the pride of Jacob</hi> by the captivity of the two tribes, as he did the pride of Israel by their captivity; He has determined to do it, to bring <hi type="italic">emptiers</hi> upon them, and the enemy that is to do it must begin with Nineveh, and reduce that first, and humble the pride of that. God is looking upon proud cities, and abasing them, even those that are nearest to him. Samaria is humbled, and Jerusalem is to be humbled, and their pride brought low; and shall not Nineveh, that proud city, be brought down too? <hi type="italic">Emptiers have emptied</hi> the cities, <hi type="italic">and marred the vine-branches</hi> in the country of Jacob and Israel; and must not the excellency of Nineveh, that is so much her pride, be turned away too? <div eID="gen20547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20548" type="x-p"/> III. A particular account given in of the terrors wherein the invading enemy shall appear against Nineveh; every thing shall contribute to make him formidable. 1. <hi type="italic">The shields of his mighty men are made red,</hi> and probably their other arms and array, as if they were already tinctured with the blood they had shed, or intended hereby to signify they would put all to the sword; they hung out a red flag, in token that they would give no quarter. 2. <hi type="italic">The valiant men are in scarlet;</hi> not only red clothes, to intimate what bloody work they designed to make, but rich clothes, to intimate the wealth of the army, and that is the sinews of war. 3. <hi type="italic">The chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation;</hi> when they are making their approaches, they shall fly as swiftly as lightning; the wheels shall strike fire upon the stones, and those that drive them shall drive furiously with a flaming indignation, as Jehu drove. Or they carried flaming torches with them in the open chariots, when they made their approach in the night, as Gideon's soldiers carried lamps in their pitchers, to be both a guide to themselves and a terror to their enemies, and with them to set all on fire wherever they went. 4. <hi type="italic">The fir-trees shall be terribly shaken;</hi> the great men of Nineveh, that overtop their neighbours, as the stately firs do the shrubs; or the very standing trees shall be made to shake by the violent concussions of the earth, which that great army shall cause. 5. The chariots of war shall be very terrible (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall rage in the streets,</hi> that is, those that drive them shall rage; you would think the chariots themselves raged; they shall be so numerous, and drive with so much fury, that even <hi type="italic">in the broad ways,</hi> where, one would think, there should be room enough, they shall <hi type="italic">jostle one another;</hi> and these iron chariots shall be made so bright that in the beams of the sun <hi type="italic">they shall seem like torches</hi> in the night; they shall <hi type="italic">run like the lightnings,</hi> so swiftly, so furiously. Nebuchadnezzar's commanders are here called his <hi type="italic">worthies,</hi> his <hi type="italic">gallants</hi> (so the margin reads it), his <hi type="italic">heroes;</hi> those <hi type="italic">he shall recount,</hi> and order them immediately and without fail to render themselves at their respective posts, for he is entering upon action, is resolved to take the field immediately, and to open the campaign with the siege of Nineveh. <hi type="italic">His worthies shall remember</hi> (so some read it); they shall be mindful of the duty of their place, and the charge they have received, and shall thereby be made so intent upon their business that they <hi type="italic">shall stumble in their walks,</hi> shall make more haste than good speed; they stumble, but shall not fall; for <hi type="italic">they shall make haste to the wall thereof,</hi> shall open the trenches; and the defence, or the covered way, shall be prepared (something to shelter them from the darts of the besieged), and they shall so closely carry on the siege, and with so much vigour, that at length the <hi type="italic">gates of the rivers shall be opened</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">v. 6</reference>); those gates of Nineveh which open upon the river Tigris (on which Nineveh was built) shall be first forced by, or betrayed to, the enemy, and by those gates they shall enter. And then the <hi type="italic">palace shall be dissolved,</hi> either the king's house or the house of Nisroch his god; the same word signifies both a palace and a temple. When the God of heaven goes forth to contend with a people, neither the palaces nor their kings, neither the temples nor their gods, can protect and shelter them, but must all inevitably fall with them. <div eID="gen20548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20549" type="x-p"/> IV. A prediction of the consequences of this; and it is easy to guess how dismal those will be. 1. The queen shall fall into the hands of the enemy (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Huzzab shall be led away captive;</hi> she that was <hi type="italic">established</hi> (so some read it), thought herself safe because she was concealed and shut up in secret, shall be <hi type="italic">discovered</hi> (so the margin reads it) and shall be led <hi type="italic">away captive,</hi> in greater disgrace than that of common prisoners; she shall be <hi type="italic">brought up</hi> in a mock state, <hi type="italic">and her maids</hi> of honour <hi type="italic">shall lead her,</hi> because she is weak and faint, not able to bear such frights and hardships, which are doubly hard and frightful to those that have not been used to them; they shall attend her, not to speak cheerfully to her and to encourage her, but murmuring and moaning themselves, as <hi type="italic">with the voice of doves,</hi> the <hi type="italic">doves of the valleys</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Ezek. vii. 16</reference>), noted for their <hi type="italic">mourning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa. xxxviii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">lix. 11</reference>. They shall be <hi type="italic">tabering upon their breasts,</hi> beating their own breasts in grief and vexation, as if they were <hi type="italic">drumming</hi> upon them, for so the word signifies. 2. The inhabitants, though numerous, shall none of them be able to make head against the invaders, or stand their ground (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nineveh is of old like a pool of water,</hi> replenished with people as a pool with water (and <hi type="italic">waters</hi> signify <hi type="italic">multitudes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Rev. xvii. 15</reference>), or as those waters with fish; it was long ago a populous city; in Jonah's time there were 120,000 little children in it (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.11">Jonah iv. 11</reference>), and, ordinarily, cities and countries are increasing in their number every year; but, though they have so many hands to be employed in the public service, yet they shall not be able to inspire one another with courage, but <hi type="italic">they shall flee away like cowards.</hi> Their commanders shall do what they can to animate them; they shall cry, "<hi type="italic">Stand, stand,</hi> have a good heart on it, and we shall do well enough;" <hi type="italic">but none shall</hi> so much as <hi type="italic">look back;</hi> they shall not have the least spark of courage remaining, but every one shall think it is his wisest course to make his best of the opportunity to escape; they shall not so much as look back to see who calls for them. Note, God can dispirit the strongest and boldest, in the day of distress, so that they shall not be what one would expect from them, but <hi type="italic">like a pool of water,</hi> the water whereof is dried up and gone. 3. The wealth of the city shall become a prey, and all its rich furniture shall fall into the hands of the victorious enemy (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">v. 9</reference>); they shall thus animate and excite one another to plunder: <hi type="italic">Take the spoil of silver; take the spoil of gold;</hi> thus the officers shall stir up the soldiers to improve their opportunity; here are silver and gold enough for them, for <hi type="italic">there is no end of the store of money and plate.</hi> Nineveh, having been <hi type="italic">of old like a pool of water,</hi> has gathered a vast deal of mud; and abundance of glory it has <hi type="italic">out of all the pleasant furniture,</hi> all the <hi type="italic">vessels of desire,</hi> which they have gloried in and which shall now be a prey and a pride to the conquerors. Note, Those who prepare raiment as the clay, and heap up silver as the dust, know not who may put on the raiment and divide the silver, <reference osisRef="Job.27.16-Job.27.17">Job xxvii. 16, 17</reference>. Thus this rich city is empty, and void, and waste, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">v. 10</reference>. See the vanity of worldly wealth; instead of defending its owners, it does but expose them, and enable their enemies to do them so much the more mischief. 4. The soldiers and people shall have no heart to appear for the defence of the city. Their spirits shall <hi type="italic">melt</hi> away like wax before the fire; their <hi type="italic">knees shall smite together</hi> (as Belshazzar's did, in his agony, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.6">Dan. v. 6</reference>), so that they shall not be able to stand their ground, no, nor to make their escape; <hi type="italic">much pain</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">in all loins,</hi> as is the case in extreme frights, so that they shall not be able to hold up their backs. And the <hi type="italic">faces of them all shall gather blackness,</hi> like that of a pot that is every day over the fire; so the word signifies. Note, Guilt in the conscience will fill men with terror in an evil day, and those who place their happiness in the wealth of this world and set their hearts upon it think themselves undone when their silver, and their gold, and their pleasant furniture are taken from them.
entries.25c892c06aba54581349d24f68d5f303495b5d5b: <div eID="gen20549" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Nineveh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the dwelling of the lions, and the feeding-place of the young lions, where the lion, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the old lion, walked, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the lion's whelp, and none made <hi type="italic">them</hi> afraid? <hi type="super">12</hi> The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard. <div eID="gen20550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20551" type="x-p"/> Here we have Nineveh's ruin, 1. Triumphed in by its neighbours, who now remember against it all the oppressions and abuse of power it had been guilty of in its pomp and prosperity (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.11-Nah.2.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where is the dwelling of the lions?</hi> It is gone; there appear no remnants, no footsteps, of it. <hi type="italic">Where is the feeding place of the young lions,</hi> where they glutted themselves with prey? The princes of Nineveh had been as lions, as beasts of prey; cruel tyrants are no better, nay, in this respect much worse—that, being men, humanity is expected from them; nay, if they were indeed lions, they would not prey upon those of their own kind. <hi type="italic">Savis inter se convenit ursæ—Fierce bears agree together.</hi> But in the shape of men they had the cruelty of lions: they walked in Nineveh as a lion in the woods, and <hi type="italic">none made them afraid;</hi> every one stood in awe of them, and they were under no apprehensions of danger from any; though nobody loved them, every body feared them, and that was all they desired. <hi type="italic">Oderint, dum metuant—Let them hate, so that they do but fear.</hi> The king himself, as well as every prince, made it his business, by all the arts of violence and extortion, to enrich himself and raise his family; he did <hi type="italic">tear in pieces enough for his whelps</hi> (and no little would be enough for them) and he <hi type="italic">strangled for his lioness,</hi> killed all that came near him, and seized what they had for his children, for his wives and concubines, and <hi type="italic">filled his holes with prey and his dens with ravin,</hi> as lions are wont to do. Note, Many make it an excuse for their rapine and injustice that they have wives and children to provide for, whereas what is so got will never do them any good; those that <hi type="italic">fear the Lord,</hi> and get what they have honestly, shall not want a competency for themselves and theirs; <hi type="italic">verily they shall be fed,</hi> when <hi type="italic">the young lions,</hi> though dens and holes were <hi type="italic">filled with prey and ravin</hi> for them, <hi type="italic">shall lack, and suffer hunger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">Ps. xxxiv. 10</reference>. 2. It is avowed by the righteous Judge of heaven and earth; it is his doing, and let all the world take notice that it is so (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord of hosts.</hi> And what good can hosts do for her in her defence, when <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts</hi> is against her for her destruction? The oppressors in Nineveh thought they only set their neighbours against them, who were not a match for them, and whom they could easily overpower; but it proved they set God against them, who is, and will be, the asserter of right and the avenger of wrong. God is against the princes of Nineveh, and then, (1.) These military preparations will stand them in no stead: <hi type="italic">I will burn their chariots in the smoke;</hi> he does not say <hi type="italic">in the fire,</hi> but, in contempt of them, the very <hi type="italic">smoke</hi> of God's indignation shall serve to burn their chariots; they shall be consumed as soon as the fire of his indignation is kindled, while as yet it does but smoke, and not flame out. Or, The drivers of the chariots shall be smothered and stifled with the smoke; then the <hi type="italic">chariots of their glory</hi> shall be the shame of their families, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa. xxii. 18</reference>. (2.) Their children, the hopes of their families, shall be cut off: <hi type="italic">The sword shall devour the young lions,</hi> whom they were so solicitous to provide for by oppression and extortion. Note, It is just with God to deprive those of their children, or (which is all one) of comfort in them, that take sinful courses to enrich them, and (as has been said of some) damn their souls to make their sons gentlemen. (3.) The wealth they have heaped up by fraud and violence shall neither be enjoyed by them nor employed for them: <hi type="italic">I will cut off thy prey from the earth;</hi> not only thou shalt not be the better for it, but no one else shall. Some understand it of the disabling of them for the future to prey upon their neighbours. (4.) Their agents abroad shall not have that respect from their neighbours and that influence upon them which sometimes they had had: <hi type="italic">The voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard,</hi> no more be heeded, which some think refers to Rabshakeh, one of Nineveh's messengers, that had blasphemed the living God, an iniquity which was remembered against Nineveh long after. Those are not worthy to be heard again that have once spoken reproachfully of God.  <chapter eID="Nah.2"/> <div eID="gen20551" type="x-p"/>

entries.7b38c34c286b68c0243e0d8e3058bb8af097fcc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12834"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Nah.2.1-Nah.2.13">Na 2:1-13</reference>. The Advance of the Destroying Forces against Nineveh, after It Was Used as God's Rod for a Time to Chastise His People: The Capture of That Lion's Dwelling, According to the Sure Word of Jehovah.</title> <div sID="gen23877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12834"/><hi type="bold">1. He that dasheth in pieces--</hi>God's "battle axe," wherewith He "breaks in pieces" His enemies. <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20">Jr 51:20</reference> applies the same Hebrew term to Nebuchadnezzar (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">Pr 25:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jr 50:23</reference>, "the hammer of the whole earth"). Here the Medo-Babylonian army under Cyaxares and Nabopolassar, that destroyed Nineveh, is prophetically meant.<div eID="gen23877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thy face--</hi>before Nineveh. Openly, so that the work of God may be manifest.<div eID="gen23878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch the way--</hi>by which the foe will attack, so as to be ready to meet him. Ironical advice; equivalent to a prophecy, Thou shalt have need to use all possible means of defense; but use what thou wilt, all will be in vain.<div eID="gen23879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make thy loins strong--</hi>The loins are the seat of strength; to gird them up is to prepare all one's strength for conflict (<reference osisRef="Job.40.7">Job 40:7</reference>). Also gird on thy sword (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8">2Sa 20:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.29">2Ki 4:29</reference>). <div eID="gen23880" type="x-p"/>
entries.6254409ab8828add0c8affba30bde388b7433a64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12835"/><div sID="gen23881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12835"/><hi type="bold">2. For the Lord hath turned away the excellency of Jacob--</hi>that is, the time for Nineveh's overthrow is ripe, because Jacob (Judah) and Israel (the ten tribes) have been sufficiently chastised. The Assyrian rod of chastisement, having done its work, is to be thrown into the fire. If God chastised Jacob and Israel with all their "excellency" (Jerusalem and the temple, which was their pre-eminent excellency above all nations in God's eyes, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.2">87:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Am 6:8</reference>), how much more will He punish fatally Nineveh, an alien to Him, and idolatrous? Maurer, not so well, translates, "restores," or "will restore the excellency of Jacob."<div eID="gen23881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">emptiers--</hi>the Assyrian spoilers.<div eID="gen23882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have emptied them out--</hi>have spoiled the Israelites and Jews (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Ho 10:1</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.16">Psa 80:8-16</reference>, on "vine branches," as applied to Israel. <div eID="gen23883" type="x-p"/>
entries.5447e0aa0773f85366299c978ff5fb26375c8144: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12836"/><div sID="gen23884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12836"/><hi type="bold">3. his mighty men--</hi>the Medo-Babylonian general's mighty men attacking Nineveh.<div eID="gen23884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made red--</hi>The ancients dyed their bull's-hide shields red, partly to strike terror into the enemy, chiefly lest the blood from wounds which they might receive should be perceived and give confidence to the foe [Calvin]. G. V. Smith conjectures that the reference is to the red reflection of the sun's rays from shields of bronze or copper, such as are found among the Assyrian remains.<div eID="gen23885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in scarlet--</hi>or crimson military tunics (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.28">Mt 27:28</reference>). Xenophon mentions that the Medes were fond of this color. The Lydians and Tyrians extracted the dye from a particular worm.<div eID="gen23886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chariots ... with flaming torches--</hi>that is, the chariots shall be like flaming torches, their wheels in lightning-like rapidity of rotation flashing light and striking sparks from the stones over which they pass (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.28">Is 5:28</reference>). English Version supposes a transposition of the Hebrew letters. It is better to translate the Hebrew as it is, "the chariots (shall be furnished) with fire-flashing scythes" (literally, "with the fire," or glitter, of iron weapons). Iron scythes were fixed at right angles to the axles and turned down, or parallel to it, inserted into the felly of the wheel. The Medes, perhaps, had such chariots, though no traces of them are found in Assyrian remains. On account of the latter fact, it may be better to translate, "the chariots (shall come) with the glitter of steel weapons" [Maurer and G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen23887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the day of his preparation--</hi>Jehovah's (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>). Or, "Medo-Babylonian commander's day of preparation for the attack" (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Na 2:1</reference>). "He" confirms this, and "his" in this verse.<div eID="gen23888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fir trees--</hi>their fir-tree lances.<div eID="gen23889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terribly shaken--</hi>branded so as to strike terror. Or, "shall be tremulous with being brandished" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23890" type="x-p"/>
entries.061a564f286afa03e51e4ff97b464d6cc31fac02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12837"/><div sID="gen23891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12837"/><hi type="bold">4. rage--</hi>are driven in furious haste (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jr 46:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justle one against another--</hi>run to and fro [Maurer].<div eID="gen23892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the broad ways--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.6">2Ch 32:6</reference>). Large open spaces in the suburbs of Nineveh.<div eID="gen23893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall seem like torches--</hi>literally, "their (feminine in Hebrew) appearance (is)": namely, the appearance of the broad places is like that of torches, through the numbers of chariots in them flashing in the sun (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.26">Pr 8:26</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen23894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run like the lightnings--</hi>with rapid violence (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">Mt 24:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.18">Lu 10:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23895" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4d56a6837776f42ae6510d63459599e91ae810b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12838"/><div sID="gen23896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12838"/>5. The Assyrian preparations for defense.<div eID="gen23896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He--</hi>the Assyrian king.<div eID="gen23897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall recount his worthies--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Na 3:18</reference>). Review, or count over in his mind, his nobles, choosing out the bravest to hasten to the walls and repel the attack. But in vain; for<div eID="gen23898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall stumble in their walk--</hi>"they shall stumble in their advance" through fear and hurry.<div eID="gen23899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the defence shall be prepared--</hi>rather, the covering machine used by besiegers to protect themselves in advancing to the wall. Such sudden transitions, as here from the besieged to the besiegers, are frequent (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.2">Eze 4:2</reference>), [Maurer]. Or, used by the besieged Assyrians [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23900" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffe3a5f96a3795ff2052a39bcdb178669743849b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12839"/><div sID="gen23901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12839"/><hi type="bold">6. The gates of the rivers ... opened--</hi>The river wall on the Tigris (the west defense of Nineveh) was 4,530 yards long. On the north, south, and east sides, there were large moats, capable of being easily filled with water from the Khosru. Traces of dams ("gates," or sluices) for regulating the supply are still visible, so that the whole city could be surrounded with a water barrier (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.8">Na 2:8</reference>). Besides, on the east, the weakest side, it was further protected by a lofty double rampart with a moat two hundred feet wide between its two parts, cut in the rocky ground. The moats or canals, flooded by the Ninevites before the siege to repel the foe, were made a dry bed to march into the city, by the foe turning the waters into a different channel: as Cyrus did in the siege of Babylon [Maurer]. In the earlier capture of Nineveh by Arbaces the Mede, and Belesis the Babylonian, Diodorus Siculus, [1.2.80], states that there was an old prophecy that it should not be taken till the river became its enemy; so in the third year of the siege, the river by a flood broke down the walls twenty furlongs, and the king thereupon burnt himself and his palace and all his concubines and wealth together, and the enemy entered by the breach in the wall. Fire and water were doubtless the means of the second destruction here foretold, as of the first.<div eID="gen23901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dissolved--</hi>by the inundation [Henderson]. Or, those in the palace shall melt with fear, namely, the king and his nobles [Grotius]. <div eID="gen23902" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee73926a8eba09909bed72f696038820cd17cc88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12840"/><div sID="gen23903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12840"/><hi type="bold">7. Huzzab--</hi>the name of the queen of Nineveh, from a Hebrew root implying that she stood by the king (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>), [Vatablus]. Rather, Nineveh personified as a queen. She who had long stood in the most supreme prosperity. Similarly Calvin. Maurer makes it not a proper name, and translates, "It is established," or "determined" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Ge 41:32</reference>). English Version is more supported by the parallelism.<div eID="gen23903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">led away captive--</hi>The Hebrew requires rather, "she is laid bare"; brought forth from the apartments where Eastern women remained secluded, and is stripped of her ornamental attire. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Is 47:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">3</reference>, where the same image of a woman with face and legs exposed is used of a city captive and dismantled (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>), [Maurer].<div eID="gen23904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought up--</hi>Her people shall be made to go up to Babylon. Compare the use of "go up" for moving from a place in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>.<div eID="gen23905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her maids ... as ... doves--</hi>As Nineveh is compared to a queen dethroned and dishonored, so she has here assigned to her in the image handmaids attending her with dove-like plaints (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Is 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">59:11</reference>. The image implies helplessness and grief suppressed, but at times breaking out). The minor cities and dependencies of Nineveh may be meant, or her captive women [Jerome]. Grotius and Maurer translate, for "lead her," "moan," or "sigh."<div eID="gen23906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabering--</hi>beating on their breasts as on a tambourine. <div eID="gen23907" type="x-p"/>
entries.12068373ab3181ea0bb43adbd31a80062529105e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12841"/><div sID="gen23908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12841"/><hi type="bold">8. But--</hi>rather, "Though" [G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen23908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of old--</hi>rather, "from the days that she hath been"; from the earliest period of her existence. Alluding to Nineveh's antiquity (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">Ge 10:11</reference>). "Though Nineveh has been of old defended by water surrounding her, yet her inhabitants shall flee away." Grotius, less probably (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.12">Na 3:8-12</reference>), interprets, the "waters" of her numerous population (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Re 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Stand, stand, shall they cry--</hi>that is, the few patriotic citizens shall cry to their fleeing countrymen; "but none looketh back," much less stops in flight, so panic-stricken are they. <div eID="gen23910" type="x-p"/>
entries.61422b3dc63f7e399e6a48d4f71be46dc75eed0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12842"/><div sID="gen23911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12842"/><hi type="bold">9. silver ... gold--</hi>The conquerors are summoned to plunder the city. Nineveh's riches arose from the annual tribute paid by so many subject states, as well as from its extensive merchandise (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.16">Na 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen23911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">store--</hi>accumulated by the plunder of subject nations. It is remarkable, that while small articles of value (bronze inlaid with gold, gems, seals, and alabaster vases) are found in the ruins of Nineveh, there are is none of gold and silver. These, as here foretold, were "taken for spoil" before the palaces were set on fire.<div eID="gen23912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory out of all the pleasant furniture--</hi>or, "there is abundance of precious vessels of every kind" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23913" type="x-p"/>
entries.91bbad6803da542a1e9065bdf490d8ed350bcf21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12843"/><div sID="gen23914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12843"/>10. Literally, "emptiness, and emptiedness, and devastation." The accumulation of substantives without a verb (as in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.2">Na 3:2</reference>), the two first of the three being derivatives of the same root, and like in sound, and the number of syllables in them increasing in a kind of climax, intensify the gloomy effectiveness of the expression. Hebrew, Bukah, Mebukah, Mebullakah (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Is 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.4">3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.15">Zep 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faces of all gather blackness--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Joel.2.6">Joe 2:6</reference>). Calvin translates, "withdraw (literally, 'gather up') their glow," or flush, that is, grow pale. This is probably the better rendering. So Maurer. <div eID="gen23915" type="x-p"/>
entries.39f92ef9e84c6f90c5aebafbd7903e8c6c6e1e94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12844"/><div sID="gen23916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12844"/><hi type="bold">11. dwelling of ... lions--</hi>Nineveh, the seat of empire of the rapacious and destructive warriors of various ranks, typified by the "lions," "young lions," "old lion" (or lioness [Maurer]), "the lion's whelp." The image is peculiarly appropriate, as lions of every form, winged, and sometimes with the head of a man, are frequent in the Assyrian sepulchres. It was as full of spoils of all nations as a lion's den is of remains of its prey. The question, "Where," &c., implies that Jehovah "would make an utter end of the place," so that its very site could not be found (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Na 1:8</reference>). It is a question expressing wonder, so incredible did it then seem. <div eID="gen23916" type="x-p"/>
entries.382d2155cbcc33175e0e2fbd3a6734b128592d55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12845"/><div sID="gen23917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12845"/><hi type="bold">12. prey ... ravin--</hi>different kinds of prey. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Is 3:1</reference>, "the stay and the staff." <div eID="gen23917" type="x-p"/>
entries.47ee94bb1a3d18a7ea3d26456cf80a75a5404adc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12846"/><div sID="gen23918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12846"/><hi type="bold">13. burn ... in the smoke--</hi>or (so as to pass) "into smoke," that is, "entirely" [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">46:9</reference>). Calvin, like English Version, explains, As soon as the flame catches, and the fire smokes, by the mere smoke I will burn her chariots.<div eID="gen23918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off thy prey from the earth--</hi>Thou shalt no more carry off prey from the nations of the earth.<div eID="gen23919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the voice of thy messengers ... no more ... heard--</hi>No more shall thy emissaries be heard throughout thy provinces conveying thy king's commands, and exacting tribute of subject nations. <chapter eID="Nah.2"/>

entries.c2a42bc5469d8b9bc5a69f6612f8663000cdcbed: <div eID="gen34993" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34994" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34995" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34995" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34994" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34996" type="x-p"/> Nineveh is now called upon to prepare for the approach of her enemies, the instruments of Jehovah's vengeance, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference>; and the military array and muster, the very arms and dress, of the Medes and Babylonians in the reigns of Cyaxares and Nabopolassar; their rapid approach to the city; the process of the siege, and the inundation of the river; the capture of the place; the captivity, lamentation, and flight of the inhabitants; the sacking of this immense, wealthy, and exceedingly populous city; and the consequent desolation and terror, are all described in the pathetic, vivid, and sublime imagery of Hebrew poetry, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.2-Nah.2.10">Nah 2:2-10</reference>. This description is succeeded by a very beautiful and expressive allegory, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11-Nah.2.12">Nah 2:11-12</reference>; which is immediately explained, and applied to the city of Nineveh, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Nah 2:13</reference>. It is thought by some commentators that the metropolitan city of the Assyrian empire is also intended by the tender and beautiful simile, in the seventh verse, of a great princess led captive, with her maids of honor attending her, bewailing her and their own condition, by beating their breasts, and by other expressions of sorrow. <div eID="gen34996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34997" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34998" type="x-p"/> He that dasheth in pieces - Or scattereth. The Chaldeans and Medes. <div eID="gen34998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34999" type="x-p"/> Keep the munition - Guard the fenced places. From this to the end of the fifth verse, the preparations made at Nineveh to repel their enemies are described. The description is exceedingly picturesque. <div eID="gen34999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35000" type="x-p"/> Watch the way - By which the enemy is most likely to approach. <div eID="gen35000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35001" type="x-p"/> Make thy loins strong - Take courage. <div eID="gen35001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35002" type="x-p"/> Fortify thy power - Muster thy troops; call in all thy allies.
entries.1bdce4be5fee91a29b7518f756dfada016645135: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35003" type="x-p"/> For the Lord hath turned away - Bishop Newcome reads, for the Lord restoreth, by a slight alteration in the text. I do not see that we gain much by this. The Lord has been opposed to Jacob, and the enemy has prevailed against him. <div eID="gen35003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35004" type="x-p"/> Emptied them out - Brought them from their own land into captivity. This was the emptying!
entries.921670cc6fc456213eae41dc174db10cf8683c7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35005" type="x-p"/> The shield of his mighty men is made red - These things may refer to the war-like preparations made by the Ninevites: they had red shields, and scarlet or purple clothing; their chariots were finely decorated, and proceeded with amazing rapidity. <div eID="gen35005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35006" type="x-p"/> The fir trees shall be terribly shaken - This may refer to the darts, arrows, and javelins, flung with destructive power.
entries.b23c291f49bd30c5f68efc304f7c58f86123ef75: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35007" type="x-p"/> The chariots shall rage - Those of the besiegers and the besieged, meeting in the streets, producing universal confusion and carnage.
entries.7c4cbd287819aa8e11aeabae31b01c041a11dabc: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35008" type="x-p"/> He shall recount his worthies - Muster up his most renowned warriors and heroes. <div eID="gen35008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35009" type="x-p"/> Shall make haste to the wall - Where they see the enemies making their most powerful attacks, in order to get possession of the city.
entries.c70638def4a4bf4e2dd64cd4b176b8b8000237e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35010" type="x-p"/> The gates of the rivers shall be opened - I have already referred to this, see the note on <reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Nah 1:8</reference>; but it will be necessary to be more particular. The account given by Diodorus Siculus, lib. ii., is very surprising. He begins thus: Ην δ' αυτῳ λογιον παραδεδομενον εκ προγονων, κ.τ.λ. - "There was a prophecy received from their forefathers, that Nineveh should not be taken till the river first became an enemy to the city. It happened in the third year of the siege, that the Euphrates [query, Tigris] being swollen with continued rains, overflowed part of the city, and threw down twenty stadia of the wall. The king then imagining that the oracle was accomplished, and that the river was now manifestly become an enemy to the city, casting aside all hope of safety, and lest he should fall into the hands of the enemy, built a large funeral pyre in the palace, (εν τοις βασιλειοις), and having collected all his gold and silver and royal vestments, together with his concubines and eunuchs, placed himself with them in a little apartment built in the pyre; burnt them, himself, and the palace together. When the death of the king (Sardanapalus) was announced by certain deserters, the enemy entered in by the breach which the waters had made, and took the city." Thus the prophecy of Nahum was literally fulfilled:" the gates of the river were opened, and the palace dissolved," i.e., burnt.
entries.ddc44f6dfbea93f53034e62c48a23a195467310d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35011" type="x-p"/> And Huzzab shall be led away captive - Perhaps Huzzab means the queen of Nineveh, who had escaped the burning mentioned above by Diodorus. As there is no account of the queen being burnt, but only of the king, the concubines, and the eunuchs, we may, therefore, naturally conclude that the queen escaped; and is represented here as brought up and delivered to the conqueror; her maids at the same time bewailing her lot. Some think Huzzab signifies Nineveh itself.
entries.e29580f4a4dd046fe5ccc910df526f0ff9f8d425: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35012" type="x-p"/> But Nineveh is of old like a pool of water - מימי mimey, from days. Bp. Newcome translates the line thus: "And the waters of Nineveh are a pool of waters." There may be reference here to the fact given in the preceding note, the overflowing of the river by which the city was primarily destroyed. <div eID="gen35012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35013" type="x-p"/> Stand, stand - Consternation shall be at its utmost height, the people shall flee in all directions; and though quarter is offered, and they are assured of safety it they remain, yet not one looketh back.
entries.a08ebe53c79b5ae9291b8ad922210a86199f8e14: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35014" type="x-p"/> Take ye the spoil - Though the king burnt his treasures, vestments, etc., he could not totally destroy the silver and the gold. Nor did he burn the riches of the city; these fell a prey to the conquerors; and there was no end of the store of glorious garments, and the most costly vessels and furniture.
entries.c006cc1a464ff6350b8a089d13d99e4df621d348: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35015" type="x-p"/> She is empty, and void, and waste - The original is strongly emphatic; the words are of the same sound; and increase in their length as they point out great, greater, and greatest desolation. בוקה ומבוקה ומבלקה <div eID="gen35015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35016" type="x-p"/> Bukah, umebukah, umebullakah. <div eID="gen35016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35017" type="x-p"/> She is void, empty, and desolate. <div eID="gen35017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35018" type="x-p"/> The faces of them all gather blackness - This marks the diseased state into which the people had been brought by reason of famine, etc.; for, as Mr. Ward justly remarks, "sickness makes a great change in the countenance of the Hindoos; so that a person who was rather fair when in health, becomes nearly black by sickness." This was a general case with the Asiatics.
entries.9c0bd1602ecbc7b84acd27ecddc5a7bef82167f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35019" type="x-p"/> Where is the dwelling of the lions - Nineveh, the habitation of bold, strong, and ferocious men. <div eID="gen35019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35020" type="x-p"/> The feeding place of the young lions - Whither her victorious and rapacious generals frequently returned to consume the produce of their success. Here they walked at large, and none made them afraid. Wheresoever they turned their arms they were victors; and all nations were afraid of them.
entries.04d18c88213f37f42c131ccd16748983a4e4fbef: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35021" type="x-p"/> The lion did tear - This verse gives us a striking picture of the manner in which the Assyrian conquests and depredations were carried on. How many people were spoiled to enrich his whelps - his sons, princes, and nobles! How many women were stripped and slain, whose spoils went to decorate his lionesses - his queen, concubines, and mistresses. And they had even more than they could assume; their holes and dens - treasure-houses, palaces, and wardrobes - were filled with ravin, the riches which they got by the plunder of towns, families, and individuals. This is a very fine allegory, and admirably well supported.
entries.8b7bde428febec48c02c328f3ccfb4fe2d5591e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35022" type="x-p"/> Behold, I am against thee - Assyria, and Nineveh its capital. I will deal with you as you have dealt with others. <div eID="gen35022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35023" type="x-p"/> The voice of thy messengers - Announcing thy splendid victories, and the vast spoils taken - shall no more be heard - thou and thy riches, and ill-got spoils, shall perish together.  <chapter eID="Nah.2"/> <div eID="gen35023" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b19f02d9f92bc4b266d38c863f93da5a75a866f: <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1-Nah.2.2">Nah 2:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen16620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference> the prophecy turns to Nineveh. Nah 2:1. <hi type="italic">“A dasher in pieces comes against thee. Keep thy fortress! Look out upon the way, fortify the loins, exert thy strength greatly!</hi> Nah 2:2. <hi type="italic">For Jehovah returneth to the eminence of Jacob as to the eminence of Israel; for plunderers have plundered them, and their vines have they thrown to the ground.” </hi>על־פּניך cannot be addressed to Judah, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah 1:15</reference> (Chald., Rashi, etc.). It cannot indeed be objected that in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah 1:15</reference> the destruction of Asshur has already been announced, since the prophet might nevertheless have returned to the time when Asshur had made war upon Judah, in order to depict its ruin with greater precision. But such an assumption does not agree with the second clause of the verse as compared with <reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Nah 2:2</reference>, and still less with the description of the approaching enemy which follows in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference>, since this is unquestionably, according to <reference osisRef="Nah.2.5">Nah 2:5</reference>, the power advancing against Nineveh, and destroying that city. We must therefore assume that we have here a sudden change in the person addressed, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.11">Nah 1:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Nah 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.13">Nah 1:13</reference> and Nah 1:14. The enemy is called מפיץ, “a dasher in pieces;” not a war-hammer (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">Pro 25:18</reference>), because עלה, the standing expression for the advance of a hostile army, does not agree with this. על־פּניך, against thy face, i.e., pitching his tent opposite to the city (there is no good reason for altering the suffix into פּניך, as Ewald and Hitzig propose). Against this enemy Nineveh is to bring all possible power of resistance. This is not irony, but simply a poetical turn given to the thought, that Nineveh will not be able to repulse this enemy any more. The <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> <hi type="italic">nâtsōr</hi> stands emphatically for the imperative, as is frequently the case, and is continued in the imperative. <hi type="italic">Metsūrâh</hi> is the enclosure of a city, hence the wall or fortification. צפּה־דרך, looking watchfully upon the way by which the enemy comes, to repulse it or prevent it from entering the city. הזּק מ, make the loins strong, i.e., equip thyself with strength, the loins being the seat of strength. The last clause expresses the same thought, and is merely added to strengthen the meaning. The explanatory <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Nah 2:2</reference> (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">3</reference>) does not follow upon <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference></hi> in the sense of “summon up all thy strength, <hi type="italic">for</hi> it is God in whose strength the enemy fights” (Strauss), but to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference></hi> or <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah 1:15</reference></hi>. The train of thought is the following: Asshur will be utterly destroyed by the enemy advancing against Nineveh, for Jehovah will re-establish the glory of Israel, which Asshur has destroyed. שׁב (perf. proph.) has not the force of the <hi type="italic">hiphil, reducere, restituere,</hi> either here or in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.5">Psa 85:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>, and other passages, where the modern lexicons give it, but means to turn round, or return to a person, and is construed with the accusative, as in Num 10:36; <reference osisRef="Exod.4.20">Exo 4:20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.50.14">Gen 50:14</reference>, although in actual fact the return of Jehovah to the eminence of Jacob involves its restoration. גּאון יעקב, that of which Jacob is proud, i.e., the eminence and greatness or glory accruing to Israel by virtue of its election to be the nation of God, which the enemy into whose power it had been given up on account of its rebellion against God had taken away (see at <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>). <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> does not stand for Judah, nor <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> for the ten tribes, for Nahum never refers to the ten tribes in distinction from Judah; and Oba 1:18, where Jacob is distinguished from the house of Joseph, is of a totally different character. Both names stand here for the whole of Israel (of the twelve tribes), and, as Cyril has shown, the distinction is this: Jacob is the natural name which the people inherited from their forefather, and Israel the spiritual name which they had received from God. Strauss gives the meaning correctly thus: Jehovah will so return to the eminence of His people, who are named after Jacob, that this eminence shall become the eminence of Israel, i.e., of the people of God; in other words, He will exalt the nation once more to the lofty eminence of its divine calling (כּ used in the same manner as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">1Sa 25:36</reference>). This will He do, because plunderers have plundered (<hi type="italic">bâqaq</hi>, <hi type="italic">evacuare</hi>) them (the Israelites), and destroyed their vines, cast them to the ground; that He may avenge the reproach cast upon His people. The plunderers are the heathen nations, especially the Assyrians. The vines are the Israelites; Israel as a people or kingdom is the vineyard (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.10">Jer 12:10</reference>; Psa 80:9.); the vines are the families, and the branches (<hi type="italic">zemōrı̄m</hi> from <hi type="italic">zemōrâh</hi>) the members.
entries.b1aa51cae02c5a5204f70e053e75829cef7b9770: <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3-Nah.2.4">Nah 2:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16622" type="x-p"/> After assigning this reason for the divine purpose concerning Asshur, the prophet proceeds in Nah 2:3. to depict the army advancing towards Nineveh, viz., in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference> its appearance, and in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.4">Nah 2:4</reference> the manner in which it sets itself in motion for battle. Nah 2:3. <hi type="italic">“The shield of His heroes is made red, the valiant men are clothed in crimson: in the fire of the steel-bosses are the chariots, on the day of His equipment; and the cypresses are swung about.</hi> Nah 2:4. <hi type="italic">The chariots rave in the streets, they run over one another on the roads; their appearance is like the torches, they run about like lightning.” </hi> The suffix attached to <hi type="italic">gibbōrēhū</hi> (His heroes) might be taken as referring to <hi type="italic">mēphı̄ts</hi> in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference> (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">2</reference>); but it is more natural to refer it to Jehovah in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Nah 2:2</reference> (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">3</reference>), as having summoned the army against Nineveh (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Isa 13:3</reference>). The shields are reddened, i.e., not radiant (Ewald), but coloured with red, and that not with the blood of enemies who have been slain (Abarbanel and Grotius), but either with red colour with which they are painted, or what is still more probable, with the copper with which they are overlaid: see Josephus, <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> xiii. 12, 5 (Hitzig). אנשׁי־חיל are not fighting men generally, i.e., soldiers, but brave men, heroes (cf. Jdg 3:29; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sa 31:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.16">2Sa 11:16</reference>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">benē chayil</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17">1Sa 18:17</reference>, etc.). מתלּעים, ἁπ. λεγ., a denom. of תּולע, <hi type="italic">coccus</hi>: clothed in coccus or crimson. The fighting dress of the nations of antiquity was frequently blood-red (see Aeliani, <hi type="italic">Var. hist.</hi> vi. 6).<note placement="foot">Valerius observes on this: “They used Poenic tunics in battle, to disguise and hide the blood of their wounds, not lest the sight of it should fill them with alarm, but lest it should inspire the enemy with confidence.”</note> <div eID="gen16622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16623" type="x-p"/> The ἁπ. λεγ. <hi type="italic">pelâdōth</hi> is certainly not used for <hi type="italic">lappı̄dı̄m</hi>, torches; but in both Arabic and Syriac <hi type="italic">paldâh</hi> signifies steel (see Ges. <hi type="italic">Lex.</hi>). But <hi type="italic">pelâdōth</hi> are not scythes, which would suggest the idea of scythe-chariots (Michaelis, Ewald, and others); for scythe-chariots were first introduced by Cyrus, and were unknown before his time to the Medes, the Syrians, the Arabians, and also to the ancient Egyptians (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.16">Jos 17:16</reference>). <hi type="italic">Pelâdōth</hi> probably denotes the steel covering of the chariots, as the Assyrian war-chariots were adorned according to the monuments with ornaments of metal.<note placement="foot">“The chariots of the Assyrians,” says Strauss, “as we see them on the monuments, glare with shining things, made either of iron or steel, battle-axes, bows, arrows, and shields, and all kinds of weapons; the horses are also ornamented with crowns and red fringes, and even the poles of the carriages are made resplendent with shining suns and moons: add to these the soldiers in armour riding in the chariots; and it could not but be the case, that when illumined by the rays of the sun above them, they would have all the appearance of flames as they flew hither and thither with great celerity.” Compare also the description of the Assyrian war-chariots given by Layard in his <hi type="italic">Nineveh and its Remains</hi>, vol. ii. p. 348.</note> <div eID="gen16623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16624" type="x-p"/> The army of the enemy presents the appearance described בּיום הכינו, in the day of his equipment. הכין, to prepare, used of the equipping of an army for an attack or for battle, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.14">Jer 46:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.14">Eze 7:14</reference>; Eze 38:7. The suffix refers to Jehovah, like that in גּבּוריהוּ; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">Isa 13:4</reference>, where Jehovah raises an army for war with Babylon. <hi type="italic">Habberōshı̄m</hi>, the cypresses, are no doubt lances or javelins made of cypress-wood (Grotius and others), not <hi type="italic">magnates</hi> (Chald., Kimchi, and others), or <hi type="italic">viri hastati</hi>. הרעלוּ, to be swung, or brandished, in the hands of the warriors equipped for battle. The army advances to the assault (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.4">Nah 2:4</reference>), and presses into the suburbs. The chariots rave (go mad) in the streets. התהולל, to behave one’s self foolishly, to rave, used here as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference> for mad driving, or driving with insane rapidity (see 2Ki 9:20). השׁתּקשׁק, <hi type="italic">hithpalel</hi> of שׁקק, to run (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.9">Joe 2:9</reference>); in the intensive form, to run over one another, i.e., to run in such a way that they appear as though they would run over one another. חוּצות and רחבות are roads and open spaces, not outside the city, but inside (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Amo 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.13-Ps.144.14">Psa 144:13-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference>), and, indeed, as we may see from what follows, in the suburbs surrounding the inner city of citadel. Their appearance (viz., that of the chariots as they drive raving about) is like torches. The feminine suffix to מראיהן can only refer to הרכב, notwithstanding the fact that elsewhere רכב is always construed as a masculine, and that it is so here in the first clauses. For the suffix cannot refer to רחבות (Hoelem. and Strauss), because הרכב is the subject in the following clause as well as in the two previous ones. The best way probably is to take it as a neuter, so that it might refer not to the chariots only, but to everything in and upon the chariots. The appearance of the chariots, as they drove about with the speed of lightning, richly ornamented with bright metal (see on <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference>), and occupied by warriors in splendid clothes and dazzling armour, might very well be compared to torches and flashing lightning. רצץ, <hi type="italic">pilel</hi> of רוּץ (not <hi type="italic">poel</hi> of רצץ, Jdg 10:8), cursitare, used of their driving with lightning-speed.
entries.a3af054d094ea0ca060ebbbfbde53e2c544ed462: <reference osisRef="Nah.2.5-Nah.2.7">Nah 2:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen16624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16625" type="x-p"/> The Assyrian tries to repel this attack, but all in vain. Nah 2:5. <hi type="italic">“He remembers his glorious ones: they stumble in their paths; they hasten to the wall of it, and the tortoise is set up.</hi> Nah 2:6. <hi type="italic">The gates are opened in the rivers, and the palace is dissolved.</hi> Nah 2:7. <hi type="italic">It is determined: she is laid bare, carried off, and her maids groan like the cry of doves, smiting on their breasts.” </hi> On the approach of the war-chariots of the enemy to the attack, the Assyrian remembers his generals and warriors, who may possibly be able to defend the city and drive back the foe. That the subject changes with <hi type="italic">yizkōr</hi>, is evident from the change in the number, i.e., from the singular as compared with the plurals in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Nah.2.4">Nah 2:4</reference>, and is placed beyond the reach of doubt by the contents of Nah 2:5., which show that the reference is to the attempt to defend the city. The subject to <hi type="italic">yizkōr</hi> is the Assyrian (בּליּעל, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference>), or the king of Asshur (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>). He remembers his glorious ones, i.e., remembers that he has <hi type="italic">'addı̄rı̄m</hi>, i.e., not merely generals (μεγιστᾶνες, lxx), but good soldiers, including the generals (as in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>; Jdg 5:13; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference>). He sends for them, but they stumble in their paths. From terror at the violent assault of the foe, their knees lose their tension (the plural <hi type="italic">hălı̄khōth</hi> is not to be corrected into the singular according to the <hi type="italic">keri</hi>, as the word always occurs in the plural). They hasten to the wall of it (Nineveh); there is הסּכך set up: i.e., literally the covering one, not the defender, <hi type="italic">praesidium militare</hi> (Hitzig), but the tortoise, <hi type="italic">testudo</hi>.<note placement="foot">Not, however, the tortoise formed by the shields of the soldiers, held close together above their heads (Liv. xxxiv. 9), since these are never found upon the Assyrian monuments (vid., Layard), but a kind of battering-ram, of which there are several different kinds, either a moveable tower, with a battering-ram, consisting of a light framework, covered with basket-work, or else a framework without any tower, either with an ornamented covering, or simply covered with skins, and moving upon four or six wheels. See the description, with illustrations, in Layard’s <hi type="italic">Nineveh</hi>, ii. pp. 366-370, and Strauss’s commentary on this passage.</note> <div eID="gen16625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16626" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s description passes rapidly from the assault upon the city wall to the capture of the city itself (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">Nah 2:6</reference>). The opened or opening gates of the rivers are neither those approaches to the city which were situated on the bank of the Tigris, and were opened by the overflowing of the river, in support of which appeal has been made to the statement of Diodor. Sic. ii. 27, that the city wall was destroyed for the space of twenty stadia by the overflowing of the Tigris; for “gates of the rivers” cannot possibly stand for gates opened by rivers. Still less can it be those roads of the city which led to the gates, and which were flooded with people instead of water (Hitzig), or with enemies, who were pressing from the gates into the city like overflowing rivers (Ros.); nor even gates through which rivers flow, i.e., sluices, namely those of the concentric canals issuing from the Tigris, with which the palace could be laid under water (Vatabl., Burck, Hitzig, ed. 1); but as Luther renders it, “gates on the waters,” i.e., situated on the rivers, or gates in the city wall, which were protected by the rivers; “gates most strongly fortified, both by nature and art” (Tuch, <hi type="italic">de Nino urbe</hi>, p. 67, Strauss, and others), for <hi type="italic">nehârōth</hi> must be understood as signifying the Tigris and its tributaries and canals. At any rate, there were such gates in Nineveh, since the city, which stood at the junction of the Khosr with the Tigris, in the slope of the (by no means steep) rocky bank, was to some extent so built in the alluvium, that the natural course of the Khosr had to be dammed off from the plain chosen for the city by three stone dams, remnants of which are still to be seen; and a canal was cut above this point, which conducted the water to the plain of the city, where it was turned both right and left into the city moats, but had a waste channel through the city. To the south, however, another small collection of waters helped to fill the trenches. “The wall on the side towards the river consisted of a slightly curved line, which connected together the mouths of the trenches, but on the land side it was built at a short distance from the trenches. The wall on the river side now borders upon meadows, which are only flooded at high water; but the soil has probably been greatly elevated, and at the time when the city was built this was certainly river” (see M. v. Niebuhr, <hi type="italic">Geschichte Assurs u. Babels</hi>, p. 280; and the outlines of the plan of the ground oh which Nineveh stood, p. 284). The words of the prophet are not to be understood as referring to any particular gate, say the western, either alone, or <hi type="italic">par excellence</hi>, as Tuch supposes, but apply quite generally to the gates of the city, since the rivers are only mentioned for the purpose of indicating the strength of the gates. As Luther has correctly explained it, “the gates of the rivers, however firm in other respects, and with no easy access, will now be easily occupied, yea, have been already opened.” The palace melts away, not, however, from the floods of water which flow through the open gates. This literal rendering of the words is irreconcilable with the situation of the palaces in Nineveh, since they were built in the form of terraces upon the tops of hills, either natural or artificial, and could not be flooded with water. The words are figurative. <hi type="italic">mūg</hi>, to melt, dissolve, i.e., to vanish through anxiety and alarm; and היכל, the palace, for the inhabitants of the palace. “When the gates, protected by the rivers, are broken open by the enemy, the palace, i.e., the reigning Nineveh, vanishes in terror” (Hitzig). For her sway has now come to an end. הצּב: the <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> of נצב, in the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, to establish, to determine (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deu 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.17">Psa 74:17</reference>; and Chald. <reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Dan 2:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.13">Dan 6:13</reference>); hence it is established, i.e., is determined, sc. by God: she will be made bare; i.e., Nineveh, the queen, or mistress of the nations, will be covered with shame. גּלּתה is not to be taken as interchangeable with the <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> הגלה, to be carried away, but means to be uncovered, after the <hi type="italic">piel</hi> to uncover, sc. the shame or nakedness (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Nah 3:5</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2-Isa.47.3">Isa 47:2-3</reference>; Hos 2:12). העלה, for העלה (see Ges. §63, Anm. 4), to be driven away, or led away, like the niph. in <reference osisRef="Jer.37.11">Jer 37:11</reference>; 2Sa 2:27.<note placement="foot">Of the different explanations that have been given of this hemistich, the supposition, which dates back as far as the Chaldee, that <hi type="italic">huzzab</hi> signifies the queen, or is the name of the queen (Ewald and Rückert), is destitute of any tenable foundation, and is no better than Hitzig’s fancy, that we should read והצּב, “and the lizard is discovered, fetched up,” and that this “reptile” is Nineveh. The objection offered to our explanation, viz., that it would only be admissible if it were immediately followed by the decretum divinum in its full extent, and not merely by one portion of it, rests upon a misinterpretation of the following words, which do not contain merely a portion of the purpose of God.</note> <div eID="gen16626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16627" type="x-p"/> The laying bare and carrying away denote the complete destruction of Nineveh. אמהתיה, <hi type="italic">ancillae ejus</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Nini</hi>. The “maids” of the city of Nineveh personified as a queen are not the states subject to her rule (Theodor., Cyr., Jerome, and others), - for throughout this chapter Nineveh is spoken of simply as the capital of the Assyrian empire, - but the inhabitants of Nineveh, who are represented as maids, mourning over the fate of their mistress. <hi type="italic">Nâhag</hi>, to pant, to sigh, for which <hi type="italic">hâgâh</hi> is used in other passages where the cooing of doves is referred to (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">Isa 59:11</reference>). כּקול יונים instead of כּיּונים, probably to express the loudness of the moaning. <hi type="italic">Tophēph</hi>, to smite, used for the smiting of the timbrels in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.26">Psa 68:26</reference>; here, to smite upon the breast. Compare <hi type="italic">pectus pugnis caedere</hi>, or <hi type="italic">palmis infestis tundere</hi> (e.g., Juv. xiii. 167; Virg. <hi type="italic">Aen.</hi> i. 481, and other passages), as an expression of violent agony in deep mourning (cf. <reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Luk 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.27">Luk 23:27</reference>). לבבהן for לבביהן is the plural, although this is generally written לבּות; and as the י is frequently omitted as a sign of the plural (cf. Ewald, §258, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), there is no good ground for reading לבבהן, as Hitzig proposes.
entries.c04b19ff3d1b857cd4394bb31da9cd49a8378793: <reference osisRef="Nah.2.8-Nah.2.10">Nah 2:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen16627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16628" type="x-p"/> At the conquest of Nineveh the numerous inhabitants flee, and the rich city is plundered. Nah 2:8. <hi type="italic">“And Nineveh like a water-pond all her days. And they flee! Stand ye, O stand! and no one turns round.</hi> Nah 2:9. <hi type="italic">Take silver as booty, take ye gold! And no end to the furnishing with immense quantity of all kinds of ornamental vessels.</hi> Nah 2:10. <hi type="italic">Emptying and devastation! and the heart has melted, and trembling of the knees, and labour pain in all loins, and the countenance of every one withdraws its ruddiness.” </hi> Nineveh is compared to a pool, not merely with reference to the multitude of men who had gathered together there, but, as water is everywhere an element of life, also with reference to the wealth and prosperity which accrued to this imperial city out of the streaming together of so many men and so many different peoples. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jer 51:13</reference>, where Babel is addressed as “Thou that dwellest on many waters, art rich in many treasures.” מימי היא, since the days that she exists. היא = אשׁר היא, the relation being indicated by the construct state; מן הוא in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference> is different. <hi type="italic">But they flee.</hi> The subject to נסים is not the waters, although <hi type="italic">nūs</hi> is applied to water in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.7">Psa 104:7</reference>, but, as what follows shows, the masses of men who are represented as water. These flee away without being stopped by the cry “Stand ye” (i.e., remain), or even paying any attention to it. <hi type="italic">Hiphnâh</hi>, lit., “to turn the back” (<hi type="italic">‛ōreph</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.39">Jer 48:39</reference>), to flee, but when applied to a person already fleeing, to turn round (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.46.5">Jer 46:5</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">Nah 2:9</reference> the conquerors are summoned to plunder, not by their generals, but by God, who speaks through the prophet. The fact is hereby indicated, “that this does not happen by chance, but because God determines to avenge the injuries inflicted upon His people” (Calvin). With ואין קצה the prophecy passes into a simple description. There is no end <hi type="italic">lattekhūnâh</hi>, to the furnishing with treasures. <hi type="italic">Tekhūnâh</hi>, from <hi type="italic">kūn</hi>, not from <hi type="italic">tâkhan</hi>, lit., the setting up, the erection of a building (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Eze 43:11</reference>); here the furnishing of Nineveh as the dwelling-place of the rulers of the world, whilst in <reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference> it is applied to the place where the throne of God has been established. In כּבד the ל might be thought of as still continuing in force (Ewald, Hitzig), but it answers better to the liveliness of the description to take כּבד as beginning a fresh sentence. כּבד written defectively, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.1">Gen 31:1</reference> : glory, equivalent to the great amount of the wealth, as in Genesis (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>). <hi type="italic">Kelē chendâh</hi>, gold and silver vessels and jewels, as in Hos 13:15. That there were immense treasures of the precious metals and of costly vessels treasured up in Nineveh, may be inferred with certainty from the accounts of ancient writers, which border on the fabulous.<note placement="foot">For proofs, see Layard’s <hi type="italic">Nineveh</hi>, ii. 415ff., and Movers, <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi> (iii. 1, pp. 40, 41). After quoting the statements of Ctesias, the latter observes that “these numbers are indeed fabulous; but they have their historical side, inasmuch as in the time of Ctesias the riches of Nineveh were estimated at an infinitely greater amount than the enormous treasures accumulated in the treasuries of the Persian empire. That the latter is quite in accordance with truth, may be inferred from the fact that the conquerors of Nineveh, the Medes and Chaldaeans, of whose immense booty, in the shape of gold, silver, and other treasures, even the prophet Nahum speaks, furnished Ecbatana and Babylon with gold and silver from the booty of Nineveh to an extent unparalleled in all history.”</note> <div eID="gen16628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16629" type="x-p"/> Of all these treasures nothing was left but desolate emptiness. This is expressed by the combination of three synonymous words. <hi type="italic">Būqâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">mebhūqâh</hi> are substantive formations from <hi type="italic">būq</hi> = <hi type="italic">bâqaq</hi>, to empty out, and are combined to strengthen the idea, like similar combinations in Zep 1:15; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.29">Eze 33:29</reference>, and Isa 29:2. <hi type="italic">Mebhullâqâh</hi> is a synonymous noun formed from the participle <hi type="italic">pual</hi>, and signifying devastation (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Isa 24:1</reference>, where even <hi type="italic">bâlaq</hi> is combined with <hi type="italic">bâqaq</hi>).
